Most shippers believe that the proposed expansion of commercial zones will decrease delay, handling loss, and damage as a result of less interlining. They believe these efficiencies should result in lower rates. Paperwork and billing procedures would also be less complicated. It is believed that service should improve for urban area shippers, particularly shippers of less-than-truckload freight, because there will be more carriers from which to choose. Zone expansion would equalize the competitive balance between urban shippers and those located in areas just outside the present zones, and the number of shippers engaging in private carriage should decline. It would also contribute to industrial development in suburban areas, thereby creating more traffic.
In addition to reiterating these general arguments, which are more fully summarized in the Interim Report, the representations of shippers, local interests, and State agencies, like those of the motor carrier interests, contained specific comments on the definition of particular zones. The cities which were the subject of the most comment are Atlanta, Ga., Denver, Colo., Los Angeles, Calif., New York, N.Y., St. Louis, Mo., the cities in the Pacific Northwest (Seattle and Vancouver, Wash., and Portland, Oreg.), port cities such as San Francisco, Calif., Houston and Galveston, Tex., Baton Rouge and Lake Charles, La., and various cities seeking consideration as twin cities.
